idea: Skill is braided from crossing strands, not climbed rung by rung — and honest practice knows which picture it is standing on.

sources.cite: Fixture, The ladder and the rope, 2026

units.text: A skill is a ladder: ordered rungs, climbed in advance-set order.

span.quote:
People say a skill is a ladder. You climb rung by rung, and the rungs are
ordered for you in advance by someone who has already climbed.

units.text: A skill is a rope: many weak crossing strands, none running the whole length.

span.quote:
It holds because many weak strands cross
each other, and no strand runs the whole length.

units.text: Ladder-trained skill collapses when the problem turns sideways.

span.quote:
A rung only bears weight in one
direction, which is why ladder-trained skill collapses the moment the problem
turns sideways.

units.text: Watch anyone good: splicing, not climbing — short strands joined until the join disappears.

span.quote: Watch anyone actually good at a thing and you see splicing, not climbing.

units.text: Practice should braid, not stack: two hours across three problems beats six up one.

span.quote:
practice should braid, not stack. Two hours across
three problems beats six hours up one.

units.text: The objection: ropes cannot be inspected; a ladder shows which rung is missing.

span.quote:
Curricula exist because ropes cannot be
inspected, and a ladder at least shows you which rung is missing.

units.text: The objection lands: a braid hides its gaps until it is loaded.

span.quote:
A braid hides its gaps until it is loaded, and by then
you are hanging from it.

units.text: Keep both pictures: climb mapped ground, braid unmapped, and know which you are on.

span.quote:
climb where the ground is mapped, braid
where it is not, and know which kind of ground you are on.

tensions.note: braid-first practice and the hidden-gaps concession pull against each other until u-8 splits the ground

gaps.label: how a braid could be inspected before it is loaded
